verdicts.evidence: An LLM (large language model) is a computer program that writes text by predicting the most likely next word, using patterns it learned from a very large amount of training text. The LLM’s knowledge is frozen at training time. It does not know about newer events or about private documents it never saw. Because it cannot see new data, the LLM can give confident but wrong answers. This problem is called hallucination. RAG solves this by retrieving relevant information from an external knowledge source and giving that information to the LLM together with the user’s question. RAG lets an LLM use up-to-date or private information without retraining the model. By providing the LLM with actual source text, RAG can reduce hallucination because the answer can be checked against the supplied documents. It does not remove hallucination completely, but it makes errors easier to spot. Preparation step (done ahead of time): Documents are split into small pieces called chunks. Each chunk is converted into an embedding, a list of numbers that represents its meaning. Texts with similar meaning get similar numbers. Answering step: The user’s question is converted into an embedding with the same method, and the most similar chunks are found. This is called retrieval. The retrieved chunks are placed in the prompt together with the question (this is called augmentation). The LLM then writes the answer (this is called generation).
